callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: Consider an activity you currently pursue without external incentives — perhaps a hobby, a personal project, or a form of intellectual inquiry. How would you respond if someone began offering you significant monetary rewards for engaging in it? Would your motivation increase, remain stable, or would something qualitative shift in how you experienced the activity? CET offers a precise theoretical answer to this question, and that answer — while initially counterintuitive — has proven remarkably robust across fifty years of empirical investigation.

callouts.title: Intrinsic Motivation (White, 1959; Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body:
Intrinsic motivation refers to the propensity to engage in activities for their inherent interest, challenge, or enjoyment — that is, for the qualitative experience of the activity itself rather than for any separable outcome or external consequence. Intrinsically motivated behavior is engaged in freely, without external pressure or inducement, and is typically characterized by higher levels of curiosity, spontaneous exploration, creativity, and willingness to persist in the face of challenge. Intrinsic motivation is not a personality trait but a functional state that is both enabled and undermined by specific psychological and interpersonal conditions.

**Boundary:** Intrinsic motivation must be distinguished from behavior that appears voluntary but is maintained by internalized external standards (introjected regulation), self-concept contingencies (ego involvement), or the anticipation of future extrinsic rewards. These involve different regulatory processes with different outcomes.

**Research Status:** Intrinsic motivation has been operationalized primarily through free-choice behavior paradigms (time spent with an activity after experimental conditions are terminated) and self-report measures. Both operationalizations have been criticized, and their relationship is not always consistent. The construct's validity is nevertheless supported by extensive convergent evidence.

**See also:** [[Extrinsic-Motivation]], [[Autonomous-Motivation]], [[Self-Determination-Theory]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Free-Choice-Behaviour]]

callouts.title: Perceived Locus of Causality (de Charms, 1968; Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body:
The perceived locus of causality refers to the subjective sense of whether an action is self-determined (internally caused) or controlled by external factors (externally caused). An internal PLOC involves experiencing one's behavior as initiated and regulated by the self — as an expression of one's own values, interests, or choices. An external PLOC involves experiencing one's behavior as pressured, constrained, or induced by forces outside the self. The PLOC construct is explicitly perceptual and functional: it does not describe the actual causal chain but the agent's interpretive experience of that chain.

**Boundary:** The PLOC is not equivalent to Rotter's [[Locus-of-Control]], which refers to beliefs about the causes of outcomes rather than the perceived cause of one's own behavior. The PLOC concerns agency over action; locus of control concerns the predictability of outcomes from action.

**Etymology:** From Latin *locus* (place) + causal (pertaining to causation). The construct names the perceived "location" of the cause of one's behavior — inside (internal) or outside (external) the self.

**Common Misconception:** It is frequently assumed that behavior is either intrinsically or extrinsically motivated in an all-or-nothing sense. The PLOC is better understood as a continuum — behavior can be experienced as more or less self-determined, and the same external event can shift the PLOC in either direction depending on the context and the individual.

**See also:** [[Autonomy-Need]], [[Autonomous-Motivation]], [[Controlled-Motivation]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[External-Regulation]]

callouts.title: Perceived Competence (White, 1959; Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body:
Perceived competence refers to the sense that one is capable of producing desired outcomes and avoiding undesired ones within a given domain — the experience of effectiveness and mastery in interaction with the environment. Within CET, perceived competence is a mediating variable: external events that convey positive information about one's capacities (competence-affirming events) tend to enhance intrinsic motivation, while events that convey negative information (competence-disconfirming events) or that undermine the sense of effectiveness tend to diminish it. Critically, the competence-enhancing effect of positive feedback is contingent upon the contextual frame being autonomy-supportive rather than controlling.

**Boundary:** Perceived competence in the CET framework must be distinguished from general [[Self-Efficacy]] (Bandura), which concerns confidence in one's capacity to execute specific behaviors toward specific outcomes. Perceived competence is a more diffuse satisfaction of a basic psychological need; self-efficacy is domain-specific and outcome-referenced.

**See also:** [[Competence-Need]], [[Self-Efficacy]], [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory]], [[Perceived-Competence]], [[Mastery-Goal]]

callouts.title: Functional Significance (Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body:
The functional significance of an external event refers to its perceived motivational role — the function the agent interprets the event as serving in relation to their behavior. CET identifies three functional aspects: (1) the *informational* aspect, in which the event conveys competence-relevant information that supports the autonomy of the individual; (2) the *controlling* aspect, in which the event applies pressure toward specific outcomes or behavioral compliance, thereby shifting the perceived locus of causality toward external; and (3) the *amotivating* aspect, in which the event conveys incompetence or signals the impossibility of effective action. Informational events tend to enhance intrinsic motivation; controlling events tend to undermine it; amotivating events tend to produce a collapse of both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation.

**Boundary:** Functional significance is not an objective property of events but a product of the individual's interpretive process. The same event — say, a competitive ranking — can serve a primarily informational function for one person (confirming their mastery) and a primarily controlling function for another (exerting pressure to maintain status). Context, individual differences in [[Causality-Orientations-Theory|causality orientations]], and the interpersonal climate of the event's delivery all influence the functional significance that is perceived.

**See also:** [[Reward-Contingency-Types]], [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Autonomy-Support]], [[Controlling-Environment]], [[Autonomy-Supportive-Environment]]

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **The Central Claim of CET**: The motivational impact of an external event is not determined by its objective properties (tangible vs. verbal, large vs. small, expected vs. unexpected) but by the functional significance the individual assigns to it — specifically, whether the event is experienced as informational and autonomy-supportive or as controlling and autonomy-undermining. The same event can have opposite effects depending on the interpretive frame the individual applies.

callouts.title: Phase II Reflective Questions
callouts.body:
1. How does the construct of "functional significance" challenge the standard assumption that rewards simply increase motivation? What does it require us to believe about how individuals process their own motivational states?
2. The distinction between perceived locus of causality and locus of control is technical but consequential. What practical difference would it make if a designer confused the two — for example, in designing a feedback system?
3. CET posits that even intrapersonal events (ego involvement) can undermine intrinsic motivation. What does this imply about the relationship between perfectionism, self-imposed standards, and the quality of engagement in a domain?

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: CET can be understood as the micro-level analysis of the macro-level SDT claim about basic psychological needs. Where SDT-BPNT (Basic Psychological Needs Theory) asks "what are the needs and why do they matter?", CET asks "what happens to these needs — specifically autonomy and competence — when specific types of external events enter the environment?" CET thus provides the mechanism that BPNT presupposes but does not itself specify.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **The Overjustification Effect as an Attribution Phenomenon**: The Lepper et al. (1973) framing draws on Kelley's attribution theory — specifically the discounting principle, which holds that the perceived role of one cause is diminished when other plausible causes are present. The salience of the external reward leads individuals to "underpercieve" their intrinsic interest as the cause, attributing their engagement primarily to the external incentive. Once the incentive is removed, the internal cause has been effectively extinguished from the person's self-understanding of their own motivation.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: The distinction between expected and unexpected rewards is one of CET's most precise and testable predictions — and one of its most counterintuitive. If rewards generally increase behavior, why would an unexpected reward fail to increase motivation but an expected reward decrease it? What does this asymmetry reveal about the psychological mechanism the theory is proposing?

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **The Cameron-Pierce Challenge to CET** rests primarily on an alternative categorization scheme for reward contingencies and a critique of the free-choice behavioral measure as the operational index of intrinsic motivation. Cameron and Pierce argued that the measure confounds intrinsic motivation with boredom satiation — that reduced engagement with a task after reward is simply the result of having performed the task multiple times, not from a reward-induced PLOC shift. The Deci et al. (1999) rebuttal showed that control groups with equivalent task exposure but no reward did not show the same reduction, which effectively refutes the satiation argument.

callouts.title: Phase III Reflective Questions
callouts.body:
1. The meta-analytic controversy between Deci et al. (1999) and Cameron and Pierce (1994) illustrates the theory-laden nature of even quantitative literature syntheses — the categorization scheme used to organize studies determines the conclusions drawn. What does this suggest about how you should interpret meta-analytic findings in motivational psychology?
2. If CET and achievement goal theory are complementary frameworks, why isn't there a single integrated theory? What does the persistence of separate theoretical traditions with overlapping claims suggest about the nature of theoretical progress in motivational psychology?
3. How does the distinction between CET (focused on how events affect intrinsic motivation) and OIT (focused on how extrinsic motivation becomes internalized) suggest that different aspects of motivation require different theoretical accounts?

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **Psychological Mediation is the Core Testable Prediction of CET**: If the theory is correct, the effects of external events on behavioral outcomes (free-choice engagement, performance quality, creativity) should be mediated by changes in perceived autonomy and perceived competence — not by direct reinforcement of behavior. This prediction distinguishes CET sharply from behaviorist accounts and generates a specific methodological requirement: tests of CET should include mediation analyses rather than only documenting input-output relationships.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Amabile et al. (1976)** showed that artists who were asked to produce artwork for extrinsic evaluation received lower creativity ratings from professional judges than those who created artwork without evaluation, and this effect was mediated by the artists' self-reports of reduced intrinsic enjoyment during the controlled condition. This early study established the creativity-undermining effect of controlling external events that has been extensively replicated.

**Grolnick and Ryan (1987)** demonstrated that children given autonomy-supportive instructions for reading a passage showed superior conceptual understanding and more durable retention compared to children given controlling instructions, despite equivalent surface-level performance — suggesting that controlled motivation produces a qualitative shift toward rote processing at the expense of meaningful encoding.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **The Functional Significance Interpretive Triangle** (original synthesis): CET's mechanism can be conceptualized as a three-point interpretive triangle in which every external event simultaneously activates three functional dimensions — informational, controlling, and amotivating — to varying degrees. The relative salience of each dimension is determined by contextual factors (the autonomy-supportiveness of the interpersonal climate), dispositional factors (the individual's causality orientation), and structural factors (the contingency architecture of the event). Effective motivational design consists of calibrating the event's architecture so that the informational dimension is dominant and the controlling dimension is minimized, which requires attention to how the event is framed, delivered, and contextualized — not only to its nominal content.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **The Interpersonal Climate as Functional Significance Amplifier**: The autonomy-supportiveness vs. controllingness of the interpersonal climate does not determine the motivational consequences of external events independently; it modulates the functional significance that those events are assigned. An event's informational vs. controlling parsing is not an objective reading of its properties but an interpretive act situated within a relational context. This is why identical reward structures can have opposite motivational effects in different interpersonal relationships.

callouts.title: Ego Involvement (Ryan & Deci, 2000; Nicholls, 1984)
callouts.body:
Ego involvement refers to a motivational state in which engagement is driven by the desire to demonstrate or prove ability rather than to develop it, where self-worth is contingently dependent on performance outcomes. Ego-involved individuals experience their engagement as controlled by internal standards that function like external pressures: the compulsion is internally generated but operates like an external contingency in shifting the perceived locus of causality from the activity's intrinsic features toward self-protective performance management. CET treats ego involvement as an intrapersonal analogue to external controlling contexts.

**Boundary:** Ego involvement must be distinguished from task involvement (focusing on mastery of the challenge itself, intrinsic to the activity) and from adaptive aspirations for excellence (which can be autonomously motivated and need-satisfying). The defining feature of ego involvement is the contingency between performance and self-worth — the stake one's fundamental sense of competence has in the outcome.

**See also:** [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Ego-Involving-Feedback]], [[Contingent-Self-Esteem]], [[Contingent-Self-Worth]], [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]], [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]]

callouts.title: Phase IV Reflective Questions
callouts.body:
1. CET proposes a mediation chain in which external events → functional significance interpretation → PLOC and competence changes → intrinsic motivation. What are the points in this chain where individual differences could produce consistent deviations from the theory's average predictions?
2. The claim that ego involvement functions like an external controlling condition is theoretically bold — it asserts that internally generated pressures can undermine intrinsic motivation through the same mechanism as external reward. What evidence would fail to support this claim, and has that evidence been found?
3. If the interpersonal climate modulates how external events are parsed, what does this imply for the design of incentive systems in organizations? Could a reward-for-performance system be designed in a way that preserves intrinsic motivation?

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**CET-Consistent Feedback Design Principles**:
(1) Prioritize informational content — be specific about what the learner did and why it worked, rather than simply evaluating whether the outcome met a standard.
(2) Preserve agency in the feedback frame — use "you found an effective approach" rather than "you did what I asked," emphasizing the learner's authorship of their performance.
(3) Minimize contingency — avoid framing feedback as the basis for future reward, punishment, or comparative ranking unless absolutely necessary, and when necessary, acknowledge the learner's perspective on the contingency.
(4) Support rather than pressure — distinguish between setting standards (informational) and pressuring toward standards (controlling).

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **The Misapplication Risk in Educational Policy**: CET is sometimes misinterpreted as a blanket indictment of all external rewards and evaluations in educational settings. This reading is both theoretically inaccurate and practically damaging. CET's predictions are contingency-specific and context-sensitive. Verbal positive feedback under autonomy-supportive conditions *enhances* intrinsic motivation. Performance standards with rationale and acknowledgment of student perspective are consistent with need satisfaction. The theory's prescriptive force targets controlling functional significance, not external events per se. Policy applications that abolish reward systems without attending to the functional significance dimensions they are designed to manage may produce environments that are structurally different but motivationally similar to what they replaced.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **Motivation as Interpretive Architecture**: CET reveals that the fundamental unit of motivational analysis is not the behavior-consequence contingency but the subjective interpretation of what a given event means for one's sense of self-determination and effectiveness. This shifts the design challenge for all motivational systems from the engineering of contingencies to the cultivation of interpretive contexts — a far more demanding but also far more powerful form of motivational technology.

callouts.title: Phase VI Integration Questions
callouts.body:
1. If CET is correct that motivation is fundamentally an interpretive achievement, what does this imply for contexts where the individual has limited interpretive agency — for example, under extreme scarcity, institutional coercion, or neurological constraint?
2. The "motivational thermodynamics" framing suggests that controlling environments impose a hidden motivational tax. How would you design a research study that could directly measure this tax — that is, quantify the motivational capital depleted by controlling contingencies relative to autonomy-supportive ones?
3. CET focuses on how environments affect individual motivation. What is the corresponding account of how individuals can develop the dispositional capacities to preserve intrinsic motivation even in controlling environments? (This connects to [[Causality-Orientations-Theory]] and the [[Self-Regulated-Learning]] literature.)

callouts.title: Cognitive Evaluation Theory — CET (Deci & Ryan, 1975, 1985)
callouts.body:
Cognitive Evaluation Theory is the mini-theory within [[Self-Determination-Theory]] that specifies the conditions under which external events — rewards, feedback, surveillance, deadlines, competitive structures — affect intrinsic motivation. CET proposes that external events have three aspects of functional significance: informational (competence-relevant, autonomy-preserving), controlling (autonomy-undermining, PLOC-shifting), and amotivating (competence-disconfirming). Informational events enhance intrinsic motivation; controlling events undermine it; amotivating events collapse it. The theory's central claims are: (1) expected tangible rewards reliably undermine intrinsic motivation for interesting activities, (2) positive verbal feedback reliably enhances intrinsic motivation, and (3) both effects are mediated by changes in perceived locus of causality and perceived competence.

**Boundary:** CET applies specifically to activities with an established intrinsic motivation baseline. It does not predict effects for activities that were never intrinsically motivated. CET also does not cover the internalization of extrinsically motivated behavior — that is OIT's domain.

**See also:** [[Self-Determination-Theory]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Overjustification-Effect]], [[Perceived-Locus-of-Causality]], [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory]]

callouts.title: Overjustification Effect (Lepper, Greene & Nisbett, 1973)
callouts.body:
The overjustification effect refers to the reduction in intrinsic motivation that occurs when an individual receives an expected extrinsic reward for engaging in an activity they were already intrinsically motivated to perform. The term derives from Kelley's attribution-theoretic discounting principle: when both an internal cause (intrinsic interest) and an external cause (extrinsic reward) are present, the individual "overjustifies" their behavior by attributing it primarily to the more salient external cause, thereby discounting the internal cause and reducing subsequent intrinsic motivation. The effect is reliably observed for expected, tangible, engagement-contingent rewards but not for unexpected rewards or verbal praise under autonomy-supportive conditions.

**Historical Note:** The term originated in Lepper et al.'s 1973 study using preschool children and reward certificates for drawing, and was originally grounded in attribution theory. Deci and Ryan later retheorized the mechanism through need satisfaction language (PLOC shift and competence modulation) rather than purely attributional inference.

**See also:** [[Overjustification-Effect]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Perceived-Locus-of-Causality]], [[Engagement-Contingent-Reward]], [[The-Undermining-Effect]]

callouts.title: Perceived Locus of Causality — PLOC (de Charms, 1968; Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body:
See full definition in Phase II. The PLOC is the subjective sense that one's behavior is self-determined (internal PLOC) or externally caused (external PLOC). In CET, controlling events shift the PLOC toward external; informational events preserve or enhance the internal PLOC. The PLOC mediates the relationship between external event type and intrinsic motivation.

**See also:** [[Perceived-Locus-of-Causality]], [[Autonomy-Need]], [[Autonomous-Motivation]], [[Controlled-Motivation]], [[External-Regulation]]

callouts.title: Functional Significance — Informational, Controlling, Amotivating (Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body:
See full definition in Phase II. Functional significance is the perceived motivational role of an external event — the function the agent interprets the event as serving. Three aspects are identified: informational (competence-affirming, autonomy-preserving), controlling (pressure toward specific outcomes), and amotivating (competence-disconfirming). The dominant aspect in an individual's interpretation determines the motivational consequence of the event.

**See also:** [[Autonomy-Support]], [[Controlling-Environment]], [[Autonomy-Supportive-Environment]], [[Reward-Contingency-Types]]

callouts.title: Autonomy-Supportive Climate (Deci, Connell & Ryan, 1989)
callouts.body:
An autonomy-supportive climate is an interpersonal context characterized by acknowledgment of the other's perspective, minimization of pressure toward specific outcomes, provision of rationale for requirements, and genuine respect for the other's agency and self-determination. Within CET, autonomy-supportive climates moderate the functional significance of external events by reducing the likelihood that any given event will be parsed as controlling. Teachers, managers, and caregivers can be trained in autonomy-supportive behavior; systematic differences in autonomy-support reliably predict differences in the intrinsic motivation, well-being, and performance of those they oversee.

**Boundary:** Autonomy-supportive does not mean permissive or unstructured. High expectations, explicit standards, and performance feedback are all compatible with an autonomy-supportive interpersonal style when they are delivered with acknowledgment and rationale. The binary of "autonomy-supportive vs. controlling" applies to the relational style, not to the presence or absence of structure.

**See also:** [[Autonomy-Support]], [[Autonomy-Supportive-Teaching-and-Learning-Environments]], [[Autonomy-Supportive-Environment]], [[Controlling-Environment]]

callouts.title: Engagement-Contingent Reward (Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999)
callouts.body:
An engagement-contingent reward is an external incentive whose receipt is conditional on engaging with the target activity — the individual receives the reward simply for working on the task, regardless of how well they perform. Within the reward contingency taxonomy of CET, engagement-contingent rewards constitute the paradigm case of the undermining effect: they introduce a controlling external contingency that transforms the activity from a spontaneous expression of interest into an instrument for obtaining an extrinsic outcome.

**See also:** [[Engagement-Contingent-Reward]], [[Reward-Contingency-Types]], [[Overjustification-Effect]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]]

callouts.title: Ego Involvement (Nicholls, 1984; Ryan & Deci, 2000)
callouts.body:
See definition in Phase IV. Ego involvement refers to a motivational state in which performance is driven by the contingency between outcome and self-worth, functioning as an intrapersonal analogue to external controlling pressure. CET predicts that ego involvement undermines intrinsic motivation through the same mechanism as external control — by shifting the perceived locus of causality from the activity's intrinsic features to self-evaluative agenda management.

**See also:** [[Ego-Involvement]], [[Ego-Involving-Feedback]], [[Contingent-Self-Esteem]], [[Contingent-Self-Worth]], [[Mastery-Goal-Orientation]]

callouts.title: Free-Choice Behavior Paradigm (Deci, 1971)
callouts.body:
The free-choice behavioral paradigm is the primary experimental operationalization of intrinsic motivation in CET research. Following an experimental manipulation (typically involving reward or feedback conditions), participants are left in a room with the target activity available along with competing options, and an experimenter covertly measures the amount of time participants spontaneously spend with the activity during an ostensibly unobserved period. The theoretical assumption is that time spent freely engaging with the activity — without any ongoing external contingency — indexes the individual's intrinsic motivation for it.

**Common Misconception:** The free-choice measure is not equivalent to self-reported interest or enjoyment, and the two operationalizations do not always converge. Meta-analyses find somewhat different patterns for free-choice behavior vs. self-report outcomes, which has generated theoretical and methodological discussion about what each measure actually captures.

**Research Status:** The free-choice paradigm has been criticized for conflating intrinsic motivation with satiation and for potential experimenter demand effects. Multiple studies use both measures simultaneously; the Deci et al. (1999) meta-analysis addressed these concerns systematically.

**See also:** [[Free-Choice-Behaviour]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation-Research-Deci-1971]]

callouts.title: Reward Contingency (Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999)
callouts.body:
Reward contingency refers to the relationship structure between a reward and the behavior or outcome for which it is delivered. CET distinguishes: task-noncontingent (reward independent of engagement), [[Engagement-Contingent-Reward|engagement-contingent]] (reward for engaging), completion-contingent (reward for finishing), and performance-contingent (reward for performing above a standard). The contingency structure determines, to a significant degree, the functional significance of the reward: engagement- and completion-contingent rewards are most reliably controlling; unexpected, task-noncontingent rewards are least likely to undermine intrinsic motivation; performance-contingent rewards have the most mixed effects, reflecting competition between informational and controlling functional aspects.

**See also:** [[Reward-Contingency-Types]], [[Engagement-Contingent-Reward]], [[Overjustification-Effect]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]]

callouts.title: Amotivation (Deci & Ryan, 1985, 2000)
callouts.body:
Amotivation refers to the absence of intentionality and volition with respect to an activity — the state in which an individual has neither intrinsic motivation nor any form of extrinsic motivation, typically resulting from repeated experiences of incompetence, learned helplessness, or the perception that no engagement with the activity can produce desired outcomes. CET identifies amotivating events — those that convey the impossibility of effective action — as producing amotivation. Amotivation is the most autonomous-need-depriving motivational state and is associated with the most negative outcomes across performance, well-being, and persistence dimensions.

**See also:** [[Amotivation]], [[Learned-Helplessness]], [[Competence-Need]], [[Self-Determination-Theory]]

callouts.title: Edward Deci (1942–2024)
callouts.body:
Professor of Psychology at the University of Rochester. Founder, with Richard Ryan, of Self-Determination Theory. Conducted the first controlled experiments demonstrating the undermining effect of external rewards on intrinsic motivation (1971). His 1975 book *Intrinsic Motivation* provided the initial theoretical architecture; the 1985 co-authored volume with Ryan *Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Determination in Human Behavior* formalized SDT including CET's seven propositions. The 1999 meta-analysis with Koestner and Ryan remains the definitive quantitative synthesis of the CET reward literature.

**Lineage:** Influenced by de Charms' (1968) Origins-Pawns distinction; White's (1959) effectance motivation; Heider's attribution theory. Influenced subsequent SDT researchers including Reeve, Vansteenkiste, Niemiec, and Grolnick.

**Relationship to Report:** Foundational — every major theoretical claim in this report traces to Deci's empirical and theoretical contributions.

callouts.title: Richard Ryan (1953–)
callouts.body:
Professor of Psychology at the Institute for Positive Psychology and Education, Australian Catholic University. Co-developer with Deci of Self-Determination Theory. Co-author of the primary SDT theoretical texts (1985, 2000). Contributed particularly to the basic psychological needs dimension of SDT, the internalization account (OIT), and the cross-cultural extension of SDT predictions.

**Lineage:** Influenced by Deci, Carl Rogers' humanistic psychology, and Jean Piaget's organismic developmental perspective.

**Relationship to Report:** Co-architect of the CET framework; responsible for deepening the psychological needs grounding of CET's mechanisms.

callouts.title: Mark Lepper (1944–)
callouts.body:
Professor of Psychology at Stanford University. Conducted the landmark "Good Player" certificate study with David Greene and Richard Nisbett (1973), coining the [[Overjustification-Effect]] and establishing the attribution-theoretic interpretation of reward undermining effects. Continued work on intrinsic motivation in educational contexts, including research on intelligent tutoring systems and motivationally adaptive instruction.

**Lineage:** Influenced by Kelley's attribution theory and Brehm's reactance theory. Worked alongside Nisbett, whose social psychological framework provided the theoretical context.

**Relationship to Report:** Provided the parallel empirical and theoretical contribution to CET from the attribution theory tradition; his framework and Deci's converged on the same phenomenon from different theoretical starting points.

callouts.title: Judith Cameron & W. David Pierce
callouts.body:
Researchers who conducted the most prominent challenge to CET's empirical claims through their 1994 meta-analysis, arguing that the undermining effect is methodologically confounded and theoretically overstated. Cameron and Pierce's work generated the most systematic methodological controversy in CET's empirical history and prompted Deci, Koestner, and Ryan's comprehensive 1999 reanalysis. Their challenge ultimately strengthened the theory by forcing greater precision about contingency structure and operational definitions.

**Lineage:** Behaviorist and neo-behaviorist tradition in learning theory.

**Relationship to Report:** Critical adversarial role — their challenges and the subsequent rebuttal define the most important empirical episode in CET's history.

callouts.title: Robert Eisenberger
callouts.body:
Professor of Psychology at the University of Delaware; researcher on learned industriousness, performance-contingent reward, and the conditions under which extrinsic rewards enhance rather than undermine motivation. Provided the most sustained theoretical alternative to CET's reward predictions, arguing that high-quality performance rewards can shape intrinsic motivation through competence confirmation and generalized application effort.

**Relationship to Report:** Alternative theoretical voice; his work on performance-contingent rewards defines one of the primary ongoing conceptual tensions in CET.

callouts.title: Wendy Grolnick
callouts.body:
Developmental researcher who extended CET to parent-child relationships and educational contexts, establishing the foundational empirical program on autonomy-supportive vs. controlling parenting and their differential effects on children's intrinsic motivation, school performance, and psychological adjustment. Her work with Ryan (1987, 1989) remains the most important early extension of CET to naturalistic educational contexts.

**Relationship to Report:** Applied translator of CET's predictions — her studies moved CET from laboratory environments to classrooms and families.

callouts.title: Informational vs. Controlling Effects of Performance-Contingent Rewards
callouts.body:
CET predicts that performance-contingent rewards have mixed effects because they carry both an informational dimension (confirming competence) and a controlling dimension (creating outcome pressure). Deci et al. (1999) found that high performance-contingent rewards produced the most variable results in the meta-analysis, with some studies showing enhancement and others showing undermining.

**Position A (CET):** The controlling functional aspect dominates in most naturally occurring performance-contingent reward contexts, producing net undermining — unless the context is strongly autonomy-supportive.

**Position B (Eisenberger):** Performance-contingent rewards that genuinely confirm high competence can enhance intrinsic motivation by satisfying the competence need without necessarily imposing controlling pressure.

**Current Evidence:** The weight of meta-analytic evidence supports CET's prediction for engagement- and completion-contingent rewards but is genuinely mixed for high-level performance-contingent rewards when autonomy-supportive framing is present.

**Why It Matters:** This tension has direct practical significance for performance management systems and educational assessment design.

**See also:** [[Reward-Contingency-Types]], [[Engagement-Contingent-Reward]], [[Autonomy-Support]], [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory]]

callouts.title: Free-Choice Behavior vs. Self-Report as Intrinsic Motivation Operationalization
callouts.body:
CET research has relied primarily on the free-choice behavioral paradigm (time spent freely with an activity) and self-reported interest as the two main operational indices of intrinsic motivation. These measures do not always converge.

**Position A:** Free-choice behavior is the more valid measure because it is behavioral rather than self-reported and is less susceptible to demand characteristics and social desirability.

**Position B:** Self-reported interest is more comprehensive, capturing the phenomenological dimension of intrinsic motivation rather than a single behavioral proxy that conflates multiple motivational and non-motivational determinants (satiation, external scheduling, etc.).

**Current Evidence:** Meta-analyses show that reward effects on free-choice behavior and self-reported interest converge in direction but often differ in magnitude, with self-report measures showing larger positive feedback effects and smaller undermining effects than behavioral measures.

**See also:** [[Free-Choice-Behaviour]], [[Intrinsic-Motivation]], [[MSLQ]]

callouts.title: The Generalizability of CET to Uninteresting Tasks
callouts.body:
CET's undermining effect predictions explicitly presuppose an established intrinsic motivation baseline. For activities that are initially tedious or aversive — tasks for which there is no baseline intrinsic motivation to undermine — does the functional significance analysis still apply, or does CET become irrelevant?

**Current Answer:** The theory explicitly acknowledges this boundary condition. For initially uninteresting tasks, the internalization account of [[Organismic-Integration-Theory]] (rather than CET) is the relevant theoretical framework. However, the practical challenge of determining which tasks have "sufficient" intrinsic motivation to be vulnerable to the undermining effect has no clear empirical resolution.

**Why It Matters:** Many educational tasks and most workplace tasks are perceived by participants as initially low in intrinsic interest. If CET applies only to a restricted range of activities, its prescriptive scope may be more limited than advocates suggest.

callouts.title: The Cross-Cultural Universality of the Undermining Effect
callouts.body:
Several studies in East Asian contexts — particularly Japan and China — have found attenuated or absent undermining effects, raising questions about whether the PLOC mechanism operates differently across cultural contexts that organize the self-environment relationship differently.

**SDT Position (Chirkov et al., 2003):** The basic psychological needs for autonomy and competence are universal; the cultural variation reflects differences in how autonomy is expressed and how relational context moderates functional significance, not differences in the underlying mechanism.

**Alternative Position:** The relative weight given to autonomous vs. controlled motivation as a default regulatory style, and the baseline functional significance assigned to authority-mediated events, may differ substantially across cultures in ways that produce genuinely different effect sizes for CET predictions.

**See also:** [[Self-Determination-Theory]], [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory]], [[Autonomy-Need]]

callouts.title: Deci, E. L. (1971). Effects of externally mediated rewards on intrinsic motivation. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 18*(1), 105–115.
callouts.body:
The founding empirical study of the CET research program. Deci's experiments with SOMA cube puzzles and monetary reward provided the first controlled evidence of the undermining effect. Essential primary source for understanding the paradigm.

**Recommended Sections:** The method section establishes the free-choice behavioral paradigm; the Discussion presents Deci's original theoretical interpretation.

callouts.title: Lepper, M. R., Greene, D., & Nisbett, R. E. (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the "overjustification" hypothesis. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 28*(1), 129–137.
callouts.body: The independent parallel discovery of the undermining effect from an attribution-theoretic perspective. The "overjustification" terminology and preschool-drawing paradigm originated here. Essential companion piece to Deci (1971).

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (1985). *Intrinsic motivation and self-determination in human behavior*. Plenum Press.
callouts.body: The primary theoretical text formalizing CET's seven propositions within the emerging SDT framework. Chapters 3–5 present the full CET architecture. Graduate-level reference for the theoretical foundations.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The "what" and "why" of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior. *Psychological Inquiry, 11*(4), 227–268.
callouts.body: The most comprehensive single-article overview of SDT, including CET's relationship to the other mini-theories. Recommended as the primary entry point into the full SDT framework post-CET.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. *Psychological Bulletin, 125*(6), 627–668.
callouts.body:
The definitive quantitative synthesis of 128 reward-intrinsic motivation experiments. Rebutted Cameron and Pierce (1994) and established the contingency-differentiated treatment of reward effects. Essential reading for understanding the empirical status of CET.

**Recommended Sections:** Tables 1–4 present the effect sizes by contingency type; Discussion addresses the Cameron-Pierce controversy.

callouts.title: Cameron, J., & Pierce, W. D. (1994). Reinforcement, reward, and intrinsic motivation: A meta-analysis. *Review of Educational Research, 64*(3), 363–423.
callouts.body: The primary empirical challenge to CET and the text that triggered the meta-analytic controversy. Read alongside Deci et al. (1999) to understand the methodological debate.

callouts.title: Grolnick, W. S., & Ryan, R. M. (1987). Autonomy in children's learning: An experimental and individual difference investigation. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52*(5), 890–898.
callouts.body: Established empirically that autonomy-supportive instructional conditions produce superior conceptual understanding and retention compared to controlling conditions, with documented motivational mediation. Core educational application study.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., Connell, J. P., & Ryan, R. M. (1989). Self-determination in a work organization. *Journal of Applied Psychology, 74*(4), 580–590.
callouts.body: Extended CET predictions to organizational contexts; manager training in autonomy-supportive behavior produced significant effects on employee intrinsic motivation, trust, and well-being. Foundational organizational psychology application.

callouts.title: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. *American Psychologist, 55*(1), 68–78.
callouts.body: Widely cited integrative overview of SDT's empirical base and practical applications. Accessible entry point; cited over 60,000 times. Key sections on autonomy-supportive contexts and learning outcomes.

callouts.title: Amabile, T. M., DeJong, W., & Lepper, M. R. (1976). Effects of externally imposed deadlines on subsequent intrinsic motivation. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 34*(1), 92–98.
callouts.body: Demonstrated that deadlines, as controlling contextual events, undermine intrinsic motivation — extending CET's predictions beyond rewards to time pressure and scheduling constraints. Important for understanding the full scope of controlling events.

callouts.title: Koestner, R., Ryan, R. M., Bernieri, F., & Holt, K. (1984). Setting limits on children's behavior: The differential effects of controlling vs. informational styles on intrinsic motivation and creativity. *Journal of Personality, 52*(3), 233–248.
callouts.body: Demonstrated that the verbal style of instructions — controlling vs. informational — modulates intrinsic motivation and creativity independently of the content of the instructions. Foundational for understanding interpersonal climate moderators.

callouts.title: Chirkov, V., Ryan, R. M., Kim, Y., & Kaplan, U. (2003). Differentiating autonomy from individualism and independence: A self-determination theory perspective on internalization of cultural orientations and well-being. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84*(1), 97–110.
callouts.body: Cross-cultural investigation of SDT's autonomy construct across four cultures; found that autonomous choice and relatedness-consistent internalization predicted well-being across cultures, supporting the universality claim while acknowledging cultural expression differences.

callouts.title: Reeve, J. (2009). Why teachers adopt a controlling motivating style toward students and how they can become more autonomy supportive. *Educational Psychologist, 44*(3), 159–175.
callouts.body: Analysis of the structural and psychological factors that lead teachers to adopt controlling styles despite the motivational costs; provides practical guidance for autonomy-supportive teaching. Combines CET with organizational constraints analysis.

callouts.title: Vansteenkiste, M., Niemiec, C. P., & Soenens, B. (2010). The development of the five mini-theories of self-determination theory: An historical overview, emerging trends, and future directions. In T. C. Urdan & S. A. Karabenick (Eds.), *The Decade Ahead: Theoretical Perspectives on Motivation and Achievement* (pp. 105–165). Emerald Group.
callouts.body: Comprehensive historical overview of the development of all five SDT mini-theories, placing CET in the context of the full theoretical development. Essential contextualizing reference.

**Claim Type Taxonomy**:
- *Empirically well-established claims* (e.g., expected tangible rewards undermine intrinsic motivation as measured by free-choice behavior; verbal positive feedback enhances it): supported by multiple independent laboratory studies and meta-analytic synthesis.
- *Theoretically well-motivated claims* (e.g., the functional significance interpretive model as the causal mechanism): consistent with the empirical patterns but not as directly testable; supported by mediation studies but not proven by them.

**Limitations**: CET's empirical foundation, while strong, rests heavily on laboratory studies with undergraduate and preschool populations. Field-based longitudinal evidence on the sustainability of reward-undermining effects is less systematic. The cross-cultural evidence base, while improving, remains smaller than the Western laboratory corpus.

callouts.body:
**Q:** What is the central claim of Cognitive Evaluation Theory regarding the effect of external rewards on intrinsic motivation?
**A:** Expected tangible rewards contingent on engaging with an interesting activity shift the perceived locus of causality from internal to external, undermining intrinsic motivation. The effect is mediated by the controlling functional significance of the reward rather than by its reinforcing value.
**Source:** Phase II — Core CET Claims
**Difficulty:** Basic
**Type:** Definition
**Tags:** CET, intrinsic-motivation, rewards, SDT

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What are the three aspects of functional significance in CET, and what are their predicted motivational consequences?
**A:** (1) *Informational*: competence-affirming, autonomy-preserving → enhances intrinsic motivation. (2) *Controlling*: autonomy-undermining, PLOC-shifting → undermines intrinsic motivation. (3) *Amotivating*: competence-disconfirming → produces amotivation (collapse of both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation).
**Source:** Phase II — Functional Significance
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Type:** Distinction
**Tags:** CET, functional-significance, intrinsic-motivation

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What is the difference between the perceived locus of causality (PLOC) and locus of control?
**A:** The PLOC concerns the perceived cause of one's *behavior* — whether one's actions are experienced as self-determined (internal PLOC) or externally caused (external PLOC). Locus of control (Rotter) concerns beliefs about the causes of *outcomes* — whether one's actions reliably produce intended results. The PLOC is about agency over action; locus of control is about the predictability of outcomes from action.
**Source:** Phase II — PLOC Definition
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Type:** Distinction
**Tags:** PLOC, locus-of-control, CET, SDT

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What does the free-choice behavioral paradigm measure, and what is your main criticism of it as an operationalization of intrinsic motivation?
**A:** It measures the time a participant spontaneously spends with a target activity during an ostensibly unmonitored period after the experimental manipulation. The primary criticism is that it may conflate intrinsic motivation with satiation, scheduling constraints, or contextual availability of competing activities — rather than purely indexing motivational state.
**Source:** Phase II — Free-Choice Paradigm definition; Phase V — Limitations
**Difficulty:** Advanced
**Type:** Process
**Tags:** free-choice-behavior, intrinsic-motivation, CET, measurement

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What is the overjustification effect, and what attribution-theoretic principle generates it?
**A:** The overjustification effect is the reduction in intrinsic motivation that follows the introduction of an expected extrinsic reward for an already-interesting activity. The attribution-theoretic principle is Kelley's discounting principle: when multiple plausible causes for an action are present, the perceived role of any single cause is reduced. The highly salient external reward "crowds out" the internal cause (intrinsic interest) in the individual's causal attribution.
**Source:** Phase III — Historical Origins; Lexicon
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Type:** Connection
**Tags:** overjustification, attribution-theory, CET, intrinsic-motivation

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** How does CET treat ego involvement? What makes it analogous to an external controlling condition?
**A:** Ego involvement is a state in which performance is driven by the contingency between outcome and self-worth. CET treats it as an *intrapersonal* controlling condition: like external controlling events, ego involvement shifts the PLOC from the intrinsic features of the activity toward a self-evaluative agenda, converting exploratory engagement into self-protective performance management. The mechanism is the same as external control — a shift in functional significance from informational to controlling — but the pressure source is internal.
**Source:** Phase IV — Ego Involvement
**Difficulty:** Advanced
**Type:** Application
**Tags:** ego-involvement, PLOC, CET, intrinsic-motivation

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What was the key finding of the Deci, Koestner, and Ryan (1999) meta-analysis regarding expected tangible rewards?
**A:** All expected tangible rewards reliably undermined intrinsic motivation as measured by free-choice behavior, across all contingency types (engagement-contingent, completion-contingent, performance-contingent). Verbal positive feedback reliably enhanced intrinsic motivation. Unexpected rewards did not significantly affect intrinsic motivation.
**Source:** Phase III — The Cameron-Pierce Controversy
**Difficulty:** Basic
**Type:** Application
**Tags:** CET, meta-analysis, rewards, intrinsic-motivation

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** How does the interpersonal climate moderate the functional significance of external events according to CET?
**A:** An autonomy-supportive climate reduces the likelihood that any given external event (including potentially controlling ones like rewards or evaluations) will be parsed as controlling in its functional significance. Conversely, a controlling climate increases the likelihood that even informationally rich events will be experienced as pressure. The climate does not determine consequences directly — it modulates how events are interpreted through the functional significance framework.
**Source:** Phase IV — Interpersonal Climate
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Type:** Process
**Tags:** autonomy-support, interpersonal-climate, functional-significance, CET

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What distinguishes engagement-contingent, completion-contingent, and performance-contingent rewards in CET's reward contingency taxonomy?
**A:** *Engagement-contingent*: reward for working on the task, regardless of performance → paradigm case of undermining. *Completion-contingent*: reward for finishing the task → undermining with additional completion pressure. *Performance-contingent*: reward for performing above a standard → most variable effects, reflecting competition between informational (competence-confirming) and controlling (outcome pressure) aspects.
**Source:** Phase III — Reward Contingency Taxonomy
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Type:** Distinction
**Tags:** reward-contingency, CET, engagement-contingent, performance-contingent

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** Why do unexpected rewards not undermine intrinsic motivation according to CET?
**A:** Because they were not anticipated during engagement, unexpected rewards cannot have been perceived as a reason for engaging in the activity. They therefore do not shift the perceived locus of causality from internal to external: the individual did not perform the activity "in order to" receive the reward, so the reward cannot retroactively reframe the motivational basis of the engagement.
**Source:** Phase III — Reward Contingency Taxonomy
**Difficulty:** Basic
**Type:** Process
**Tags:** CET, unexpected-reward, PLOC, intrinsic-motivation

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** How does CET relate to Basic Psychological Needs Theory (BPNT) within SDT?
**A:** BPNT specifies that autonomy and competence (and relatedness) are universal psychological needs whose satisfaction is necessary for well-being and effective functioning. CET provides the micro-level specification of how environmental events either satisfy or frustrate the needs for autonomy (via PLOC) and competence (via perceived competence modulation). CET is the mechanism through which BPNT operates at the level of specific external events.
**Source:** Phase III — CET within SDT
**Difficulty:** Advanced
**Type:** Connection
**Tags:** CET, BPNT, SDT, basic-psychological-needs

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What is CET's prediction about the effect of verbal positive feedback on intrinsic motivation, and what is the key conditioning factor?
**A:** Verbal positive feedback reliably enhances intrinsic motivation because it satisfies the competence need without imposing controlling pressure. The key conditioning factor is the interpersonal climate: if the context in which the feedback is delivered is autonomy-supportive, the informational aspect dominates and intrinsic motivation is enhanced. If the context is controlling — even when the content of the feedback is positive — the controlling aspect may compete with or override the informational aspect.
**Source:** Phase II — Propositions; Phase IV — Mechanisms
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Type:** Application
**Tags:** verbal-feedback, intrinsic-motivation, autonomy-support, CET

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** What is the "motivational tax" metaphor as used in this report, and what does it describe?
**A:** The "motivational tax" refers to the depletion of intrinsic motivational capital that controlling environments impose on participants. Even when controlling systems achieve behavioral compliance (outputs are produced), they simultaneously consume the autonomous motivational resources that drive creative, self-sustaining, deep performance. The metaphor captures CET's core warning: systems that maximize short-term behavioral output through control may systematically undermine the intrinsic motivational substrate on which long-term, high-quality performance depends.
**Source:** Phase VI — Synthesis
**Difficulty:** Advanced
**Type:** Connection
**Tags:** CET, motivational-tax, autonomous-motivation, intrinsic-motivation

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Q:** How does CET distinguish its account of the overjustification effect from Lepper et al.'s original attribution-theoretic framing?
**A:** Lepper et al. grounded the overjustification effect in Kelley's discounting principle — the external reward crowds out the internal cause in attributional inference. Deci and Ryan retheorized the mechanism through need-satisfaction language: the controlling event shifts the perceived locus of causality (frustrating autonomy need) and modulates perceived competence (either supporting or frustrating the competence need). The need-satisfaction account generates additional predictions about well-being and affect that the purely attributional account cannot produce — specifically, that the quality of subjective experience (not just behavior) should be degraded by controlling conditions.
**Source:** Phase III — CET in Relation to Other Frameworks
**Difficulty:** Advanced
**Type:** Distinction
**Tags:** CET, overjustification, attribution-theory, SDT, psychological-needs

- *Description*: The SDT mini-theory that accounts for stable individual differences in how people interpret external events — specifically, whether their default orientation is to parse events as autonomy-supportive (autonomous orientation), controlling (controlled orientation), or amotivating (impersonal orientation). These orientations moderate the functional significance mechanism at the heart of CET.
- *Connection to This Report*: Causality orientations explain why identical external events produce different motivational effects for different individuals — filling the individual difference gap in CET's mechanistic account.

- *Description*: A practical focused analysis of how CET and related SDT principles can be operationalized in feedback design, covering informational vs. controlling feedback styles, process praise vs. person/outcome praise, the role of rationale in reducing controlling salience, and the design of rubrics and evaluation frameworks that preserve autonomy while maintaining standards.
- *Connection to This Report*: Feedback design is the most direct applied domain of CET; this expansion provides the design-oriented complement to the theoretical treatment.

- *Description*: Analysis of how classroom and organizational motivational climate — the cumulative effect of task structures, authority structures, recognition systems, grouping practices, evaluation procedures, and time allocation — shapes the functional significance of environmental events. The TARGET framework (Ames, 1992) provides the most systematic operationalization of CET predictions at the systemic level.
- *Connection to This Report*: Motivational climate is the macro-level structural expression of CET's interpersonal climate construct; understanding it provides the systems-level design complement to CET's dyadic focus.
- *Priority*: Medium
- *Suggested Report Type*: Focused Analysis Report

- *Description*: Investigation of attribution retraining interventions — structured programs designed to shift attributional patterns from external, unstable, or entity-fixed attributions toward internal, controllable, incremental ones. These interventions address the PLOC construct from the intervention side: rather than designing environments to preserve internal PLOC, they work at the level of the individual's interpretive habits.
- *Connection to This Report*: Attribution retraining addresses the same psychological substrate (PLOC and competence beliefs) that CET analyzes at the environmental level; understanding it provides the person-focused complement to CET's environment-focused prescriptions.
- *Priority*: Medium
- *Suggested Report Type*: Focused Analysis Report

wiki_links.section: Phase I: Orientation & Context Setting
wiki_links.context_line: One of the most consequential and counterintuitive findings in twentieth-century motivational psychology is that rewarding people for activities they already enjoy can — under specifiable and now well-understood conditions — systematically destroy their motivation to engage in those activities. This finding, which emerged from Edward Deci's early laboratory experiments in the 1970s and was subsequently given theoretical architecture through [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory]], challenged decades of behaviorist assumptions about the universally reinforcing function of rewards and redirected the study of motivation toward an examination of the qualitative experience of engagement itself.

wiki_links.section: Phase I: Orientation & Context Setting
wiki_links.context_line: [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory]] (CET) is a mini-theory within the macro-framework of [[Self-Determination-Theory]] (SDT), developed by [[Edward-Deci]] and [[Richard-Ryan]] to explain how external events — including tangible rewards, verbal praise, feedback, surveillance, deadlines, and competitive structures — affect the quality and durability of [[Intrinsic-Motivation]]. CET does not treat all external events as equivalent in their motivational consequences. Instead, it proposes that the motivational impact of any external event depends on the functional significance that the recipient ascribes to the event — specifically, whether the event is experienced as providing information about competence or as exerting control over behavior.

wiki_links.section: Scope of This Report
wiki_links.context_line: This foundational report provides comprehensive treatment of Cognitive Evaluation Theory across its theoretical architecture, empirical foundations, mechanistic account, and practical implications. It covers CET's core constructs — [[Perceived-Locus-of-Causality]], perceived competence, and the functional significance of external events — its seven formal propositions as articulated by Deci and Ryan, the reward contingency taxonomy through which different reward structures are predicted to have differential effects, the protracted empirical debate over the theory's validity, and its integration within the broader SDT framework and the landscape of motivational psychology.

wiki_links.section: The Problem CET Was Designed to Solve
wiki_links.context_line: To understand [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory]], it is necessary to understand the theoretical problem it was constructed to address. By the time [[Edward-Deci]] began his experimental program in the early 1970s, motivational psychology was dominated by behaviorist assumptions. Reinforcement theory, drawing from Thorndike's law of effect and Skinner's operant conditioning program, held that behavior is a function of its consequences: behaviors followed by rewards increase in frequency, and the stronger or more consistent the reward, the more firmly the behavior is established. On this account, motivation is essentially synonymous with the external contingencies that regulate behavior — an assumption that leaves no conceptual room for the distinction between intrinsically and extrinsically motivated behavior, because all behavior is, in effect, extrinsically maintained.

wiki_links.section: The Problem CET Was Designed to Solve
wiki_links.context_line: The problem with this view was that it could not account for a category of behavior that was both empirically obvious and theoretically significant: behavior undertaken for its own sake, in the absence of any external contingency. People engage in exploration, play, artistic creation, and intellectual inquiry without any apparent external incentive, and often with high levels of sustained engagement, creativity, and performance quality. The concept of [[Intrinsic-Motivation]] — the propensity to engage in activities because they are inherently interesting, enjoyable, or satisfying — had been proposed by Robert White (1959) under the rubric of "effectance motivation" and been taken up by cognitive theorists, but it lacked the theoretical precision needed to generate testable predictions.

wiki_links.section: The Perceived Locus of Causality
wiki_links.context_line: The first and arguably most foundational construct in CET is the [[Perceived-Locus-of-Causality]] (PLOC), adapted from de Charms' (1968) distinction between "Origins" and "Pawns." An individual who perceives themselves as the origin of their behavior — who experiences their engagement as self-determined and internally caused — has an internal PLOC. An individual who perceives their behavior as caused by external forces, pressures, or contingencies — who experiences themselves as a pawn of extrinsic circumstances — has an external PLOC.

wiki_links.section: The Perceived Locus of Causality
wiki_links.context_line: > **Boundary:** The PLOC is not equivalent to Rotter's [[Locus-of-Control]], which refers to beliefs about the causes of outcomes rather than the perceived cause of one's own behavior. The PLOC concerns agency over action; locus of control concerns the predictability of outcomes from action.

wiki_links.context_line: The second core construct in CET is perceived competence — the sense of being effective and capable in one's interactions with the environment. Situating CET Within the SDT Family
wiki_links.context_line: [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory]] occupies a specific analytical niche within the SDT framework. SDT, as a macro-theory, comprises six interrelated mini-theories, each addressing a different facet of motivation and personality. CET is specifically concerned with the conditions under which [[Intrinsic-Motivation]] is maintained, enhanced, or undermined by external events. It does not address — and explicitly declines to address — the full internalization spectrum for extrinsically motivated behavior, which is the province of [[Organismic-Integration-Theory]] (OIT). The relationship between CET and OIT is complementary: CET explains what happens to intrinsic motivation when the environment introduces external events; OIT explains how initially external motivation can become progressively internalized and autonomous through a developmental process.

wiki_links.section: The Historical Origins: Deci's Early Experiments
wiki_links.context_line: Simultaneously and independently, Lepper, Greene, and Nisbett (1973) conducted the now-classic "expected reward" study with preschool children who enjoyed drawing. Children in the expected award condition who drew pictures to receive a "Good Player" certificate subsequently showed significantly less spontaneous drawing behavior in a naturalistic classroom setting. Their study introduced the term [[Overjustification-Effect]], derived from attribution theory: the child who receives an expected external reward for an enjoyable activity has an excess of justification for their engagement — both the intrinsic enjoyment and the extrinsic reward — and attribution principles predict that the more salient external cause (the reward) will be assigned causal priority, effectively "crowding out" the intrinsic cause.

wiki_links.section: The Reward Contingency Taxonomy
wiki_links.context_line: **Engagement-contingent rewards**: Rewards contingent on engaging with the task but not on how well it is performed (e.g., "You can earn a reward for working on these puzzles"). These are predicted to undermine intrinsic motivation because they transform engagement from a spontaneous act into an instrumental means toward an end. The [[Engagement-Contingent-Reward]] is the paradigm case of the undermining effect.

wiki_links.section: CET in Relation to Other Motivational Frameworks
wiki_links.context_line: **In relation to [[Achievement-Goal-Theory]]**: Achievement goal theory, associated with Elliot and Harackiewicz building on Dweck and Ames, distinguishes between mastery goals (focused on learning and personal improvement) and performance goals (focused on demonstrating ability relative to others). CET's prediction that controlling, performance-focused contexts undermine intrinsic motivation maps onto achievement goal theory's finding that ego-involving, performance-approach and performance-avoidance goal contexts are associated with reduced intrinsic motivation and diminished deep processing. The frameworks are complementary and mutually reinforcing, with CET providing the psychological mechanism (PLOC shift and competence need frustration) through which goal structures produce their motivational effects.

wiki_links.section: CET in Relation to Other Motivational Frameworks
wiki_links.context_line: **In relation to [[Attribution-Theory]]**: The overlap between CET and attribution theory, particularly the application of the discounting principle to intrinsic motivation, was recognized by both Deci and Lepper et al. from the outset. However, CET departs from pure attribution theory by grounding the mechanism in basic psychological needs (autonomy and competence) rather than in attributional inference per se. This distinction is theoretically significant: need-satisfaction dynamics are not reducible to cognitive attributional operations and carry additional predictions about well-being and affect that attribution theory alone cannot generate.

wiki_links.section: CET in Relation to Other Motivational Frameworks
wiki_links.context_line: **In relation to [[Growth-Mindset]] theory**: Dweck's entity/incremental theory of intelligence framework generates predictions that partially overlap with CET. The claim that entity theory environments (which signal that intelligence is fixed and being evaluated) produce defensive motivational orientations is congruent with CET's claim that ego-involving, controlling environments undermine intrinsic motivation. However, CET provides the motivational process account — through needs for autonomy and competence — that Dweck's framework does not specify.

wiki_links.section: The Psychological Mediation Chain
wiki_links.context_line: CET's mechanistic account is relatively explicit compared to many motivational theories. The theory specifies a three-step causal chain: (1) an external event enters the environment; (2) the individual interprets the functional significance of the event through their perception of its informational versus controlling properties; (3) this interpretation modulates the two psychological mediators — [[Perceived-Locus-of-Causality|perceived locus of causality]] and perceived competence — which in turn determine whether intrinsic motivation is enhanced, maintained, or undermined.

wiki_links.section: The Psychological Mediation Chain
wiki_links.context_line: This chain is not automatic. The same objective event can traverse it in different directions depending on contextual moderators (the interpersonal climate in which the event occurs), dispositional moderators (the individual's [[Causality-Orientations-Theory|causality orientations]], which dispose them to interpret events as informational or controlling), and the domain-specific history of autonomous engagement (whether the activity has a baseline of intrinsic motivation that can be undermined).

wiki_links.section: How Informational Events Enhance Intrinsic Motivation
wiki_links.context_line: The mechanism through which informational events enhance intrinsic motivation is distinct and requires separate analysis. When an external event is parsed primarily as informational — when it conveys accurate, sincere feedback about the individual's competence without imposing pressure or contingent obligation — it supports both mediators in CET's model. It enhances perceived competence by confirming effective engagement, and it preserves the internal [[Perceived-Locus-of-Causality|perceived locus of causality]] because the feedback is experienced as consistent with and supportive of the individual's own evaluative framework rather than as redirecting their behavior toward an externally imposed standard.

wiki_links.section: The Role of the Interpersonal Climate
wiki_links.context_line: [[Autonomy-Support]] in this technical sense does not mean the absence of structure, standards, or requirements. An autonomy-supportive teacher can set high expectations, provide explicit standards, and offer corrective feedback — without these becoming controlling in their functional significance — provided that they are delivered with acknowledgment of the student's perspective and without pressure toward specific behaviors. Conversely, a teacher who offers rewards and praise but in a pressuring, surveillant, and conditionally approving manner will undermine intrinsic motivation despite the ostensibly positive valence of the events.

Educational Applications
wiki_links.context_line: **Feedback design**: CET strongly predicts that feedback should be informational in its functional significance — conveying genuine information about competence and progress without exerting pressure toward specific performance outcomes. [[Process-Praise]] (praising the effort, strategy, or approach rather than the outcome or person) aligns with CET's requirements: it is informational (it identifies what contributed to effective performance), autonomy-preserving (it acknowledges the learner's agency), and competence-supporting without being contingency-creating. In contrast, person-level praise ("You are so talented") or outcome-contingent praise ("You'd better keep performing this well if you want to maintain your standing") activates the controlling functional aspect. The [[Feedback-Design]] literature has increasingly converged on CET-consistent principles for this reason.

This literature represents one of the most robust applied extensions of CET.

wiki_links.section: The Integration with SDT's Broader Ecosystem
wiki_links.context_line: The deepest value of CET as a theoretical contribution lies not in its specific predictions about reward effects but in its role as the mechanistic bridge within SDT's theoretical ecosystem. CET operationalizes what basic need satisfaction actually means at the level of specific environmental inputs. [[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory]] tells us that [[Autonomy-Need|autonomy]] and [[Competence-Need|competence]] are universal needs; [[Organismic-Integration-Theory]] tells us how extrinsically motivated behavior can become progressively autonomous; [[Causality-Orientations-Theory]] tells us how dispositional tendencies to interpret events as autonomy-supportive or controlling moderate all of these effects. CET provides the micro-level specification of how individual environmental events either nourish or frustrate the needs that all of these frameworks reference.

[[Basic-Psychological-Needs-Theory]] tells us that [[Autonomy-Need|autonomy]] and [[Competence-Need|competence]] are universal needs; [[Organismic-Integration-Theory]] tells us how extrinsically motivated behavior can become progressively autonomous; [[Causality-Orientations-Theory]] tells us how dispositional tendencies to interpret events as autonomy-supportive or controlling moderate all of these effects. CET provides the micro-level specification of how individual environmental events either nourish or frustrate the needs that all of these frameworks reference.

wiki_links.context_line: > Cognitive Evaluation Theory is the mini-theory within [[Self-Determination-Theory]] that specifies the conditions under which external events — rewards, feedback, surveillance, deadlines, competitive structures — affect intrinsic motivation. CET proposes that external events have three aspects of functional significance: informational (competence-relevant, autonomy-preserving), controlling (autonomy-undermining, PLOC-shifting), and amotivating (competence-disconfirming). Informational events enhance intrinsic motivation; controlling events undermine it; amotivating events collapse it. The theory's central claims are: (1) expected tangible rewards reliably undermine intrinsic motivation for interesting activities, (2) positive verbal feedback reliably enhances intrinsic motivation, and (3) both effects are mediated by changes in perceived locus of causality and perceived competence.

wiki_links.context_line: > Reward contingency refers to the relationship structure between a reward and the behavior or outcome for which it is delivered. CET distinguishes: task-noncontingent (reward independent of engagement), [[Engagement-Contingent-Reward|engagement-contingent]] (reward for engaging), completion-contingent (reward for finishing), and performance-contingent (reward for performing above a standard). The contingency structure determines, to a significant degree, the functional significance of the reward: engagement- and completion-contingent rewards are most reliably controlling; unexpected, task-noncontingent rewards are least likely to undermine intrinsic motivation; performance-contingent rewards have the most mixed effects, reflecting competition between informational and controlling functional aspects.
